title: Materials
text:
Guides, documentation, and teaching notes. These currently cover phdid, my R package for partial homogeneity in staggered difference-in-differences. I will be adding notes on economics studies and coding here as I go.



phdid Vignettes




Written to walk someone through empirical applications of the package in R.




phdid vignette


Minimum Wages and Teen Employment: Recovering Partial Homogeneity


Walks through the county-level minimum wage analysis of Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021): taking cohort-time effects from did::att_gt(), testing whether there is heterogeneity worth recovering, and grouping the effects with both a point partition and a Dirichlet Process posterior.

Read the vignette 



phdid vignette


When Partial Homogeneity Helps, and When It Does Not


A reduced-scale Monte Carlo showing how the precision gains from pooling cohort-time effects depend on how well separated those effects are, and how the estimators compare on variance, bias, and interval coverage.

Read the vignette

title: Research
text:
Working Papers





2026



A Bayesian Approach to Partial Homogeneity in Staggered Difference-in-Differences


with Parush Arora


Software: phdid — an R package implementing the paper’s estimators and diagnostics, available on CRAN. Vignettes and documentation are under Materials.


ABS PDF  phdid package & vignettes



Abstract: Addresses heterogeneous treatment effect estimation in staggered difference-in-differences designs, where existing approaches force a choice between an inefficient, fully-flexible estimator or a biased pooled one. We instead use a Dirichlet Process mixture model to identify natural groupings among cohort-time treatment effects, delivering point estimates, credible intervals, and co-clustering probabilities via a collapsed Gibbs sampler. Simulations show 26–52% variance reduction relative to standard flexible estimators while maintaining near-nominal coverage.







Other Projects





2026



AI Adoption and Human Capital Formation in Developing Economies (Work in Progress)


ABS PDF



Abstract: Develops a tractable theoretical framework combining task-based automation models (Acemoglu and Restrepo) with search-friction models of skill formation (Wasmer; Acemoglu) to study AI adoption in developing economies. The model identifies an “AI learning gap”: as general-purpose AI becomes more reliable, it simultaneously erodes workers’ incentive to acquire specialized, AI-complementary skills and firms’ incentive to train them — a dynamic that can trap the economy in a low-skill equilibrium. Derives comparative statics, three possible steady states, and testable empirical predictions.






2026



Mobility Shocks and Employment Outcomes during COVID-19


with Yash Khaitan and Shagun Khetan


ABS PDF  CODE



Abstract: Combines individual-level panel data from the Consumer Pyramids Household Survey with district-level Google mobility data to study how lockdown-induced mobility shocks affected employment in India, using a difference-in-differences design with individual and time fixed effects. Average employment effects are modest but mask sharp heterogeneity: losses are concentrated among the lowest income quartile and among salaried/self-employed workers, and are driven primarily by increased job exits rather than reduced hiring. Wage declines among those who remain employed are substantial, particularly for women.






2026



Dimensionality Reduction for Sparse Movie Ratings Data: PCA via Efficient Power Method Implementation


ABS PDF  CODE  INTERACTIVE PLOT



Abstract: Implements a Simultaneous Power Method with an “implicit centering” modification to compute PCA on the highly sparse (93.7%) MovieLens 100K ratings matrix without ever densifying it. The recovered components yield interpretable latent axes of movie taste — market engagement versus critical-acclaim-vs-blockbuster preference — and are used to test how users’ positions along these axes relate to age and gender.






2025



Using Data Mining to Predict Secondary School Student Performance: A Replication and Extension


with Aditya Kumar, Rutupurna Debalina Naik, and Sidra Shaikh


ABS PDF  CODE



Summary: Replicates Cortez and Silva’s (2008) study on predicting secondary-school final grades from school, social, and demographic data, confirming the original performance hierarchy across Decision Tree, SVM, and Random Forest models. Extends the work with wrapper- and filter-based feature selection, showing that a small set of 9–23 “core predictors” matches or beats the original 30+ feature models once prior grades are unavailable — with the largest gains for the SVM, consistent with its known sensitivity to irrelevant inputs.

title: Rohan Wagle
text:
Welcome!
I am a final-year B.A. (Hons. with Research) Economics student and completing a minor in Mathematics at Ashoka University.
My academic and research interests center on empirical questions within labour economics, development economics and firm dynamics. I am particularly drawn to the intersection of applied econometrics with data science and machine learning techniques to draw out causal insights from micro-level data.
Throughout my undergraduate studies, I have balanced my coursework with research roles and projects spanning fieldwork and computational domains. Currently, I am working on my final-year thesis on the firm-level effects of Artificial Intelligence in India.
Work aside, I deeply enjoy reading modern history and philosophical texts, listening to and playing music across genres, and writing introspective long-form articles.
